title: The man on the lane in Kashi
hookLine: on a narrow lane in Kashi, the great teacher tells a man to step aside, and the man asks who should move
carry: the same self lives in everyone
tomorrow: The boy bent in eight places

cards: There's a story told about Shankara in Varanasi, the holy city also called Kashi.
He's walking to the river with his students, and on a narrow lane a man comes toward them with his dogs, a man from a community that the purity rules of the day kept at a distance.
Shankara says what the custom said to say: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks: which should move away from which?
This body from that body? Both are made of food. Or this self from that self?

teach.h: WHOEVER SEES THIS WAY IS MY TEACHER.
teach.b: Tradition says Shankara then composed five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, each ending, roughly: whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth. Here's the teaching under the story.
If your real self, the atman, isn't the body, then it's the same awareness in everyone: the monk, the man with the dogs, and you.
The Gita says it too: the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and the one who eats dogs. Hindu society did draw hard lines of caste and purity, and that history is real.
Many Hindus today point to this story when they say those lines never reach the self. Shankara taught the one self for years, and it took a stranger to make him live it. Knowing isn't living.
So texts in his tradition, like the Vivekachudamani, list four qualities a student needs.
Viveka: telling the lasting from the passing.
Vairagya: loosening your grip on what passes. A steady mind: calm, patience, trust, focus. And “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.

Viveka caught up with Shankara on the lane: the rule was about bodies, and the self is not a body. And today? Think of the person you're quick to rank below you: the new kid, the cleaner, the one with the accent.

teach.h: THE SAME SELF LIVES IN EVERYONE.
teach.b: The same self is looking out of their eyes.

how: Advaita teachers say the one self (atman) is the same in every being, and tell the Kashi story of Shankara to show it; students also work on four qualifications (sadhana chatushtaya): discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues of a steady mind, and longing for freedom.

o: knowing the one self in everyone, whatever their birth
a set of purity rules about who must step aside for whom
hard study that only very clever people can ever manage

games.q: the four qualifications — tap the pairs.
p: which self should move from which?
five verses after the lane in Kashi

s: in the story, Shankara convinces the man to step aside
the man asks which should move from which, body or self, and Shankara bows to him.
in the story, Shankara decides the rule was right but bows to be polite
he sees the rule was about bodies, while the self in both of them is one, and calls such a seer his teacher.
the Vivekachudamani says the other virtues need dispassion and longing for freedom behind them
where those two are weak, it says, calm and the rest are like water seen in a desert.

games.q: you're Shankara on the lane. the man with the dogs asks: should this body move from that body, both made of food, or this self from that self? what does the story say you do?
games.why: he bows. tradition says he then wrote five verses honoring anyone who sees this way, whatever their birth.

practice: Sort things gently as they arise: a sound, passing; a twinge in the knee, passing; a worry about tomorrow, a pleasant memory, passing too.

Don't push any of it away; then notice what hasn't passed through all of it, the noticing, and rest there for a few breaths. If you want, remember the man on the lane, and let there be no one to step aside from.

wordCard.voice: Jnana yoga, on the lane in Kashi: the same self in everyone. Its students need four qualities: viveka, telling lasting from passing; vairagya, dispassion; a steady mind; and “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.

orig.note: Sanskrit: viveka, discernment, telling apart; the first of the four qualifications, and the word in Vivekachudamani.

carryVoice: Your line: the same self lives in everyone. On a lane in Kashi, it came back as a question: which should move from which? Two seventy-seven, done.

sources.ref: Manisha Panchakam (attributed to Shankara) and the Kashi story in the Shankara-digvijaya tradition
Vivekachudamani (attributed to Shankara), the four qualifications
